articles.title: My Release Pipeline Refused to Ship My Release. It Was Right.
articles.description: I pushed the v0.2.0 tag. The release workflow built the wheel, generated the SBOM, wrote the...
articles.body_html:
I pushed the v0.2.0 tag. The release workflow built the wheel, generated the SBOM, wrote the checksums, signed everything with keyless Sigstore — and then failed at its own last step:

X Verify the release before publishing
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'cryptography'

The workflow never published. GitHub release: absent. That is the system working exactly as designed, and this is the story of the bug it caught — one my test suite structurally could not have caught, in a place I'd stopped thinking about years ago.

This is from the agentwatch v0.2.1 release — the agent-security tool in agentsec-ecosystem. Repo: agentsec-ecosystem/agentwatch.

The design that saved the release

The release workflow has a step before publishing: install the package and run agentwatch verify-release — re-verify the built artifacts from inside a clean environment. The workflow file documents its own contract in one line:

The workflow refuses to publish an artifact that agentwatch verify-release cannot confirm.

It's not a smoke test. It's a publication precondition. If the CLI can't run, nothing ships. So when the CLI couldn't run, the only thing that shipped that day was... nothing.

That single design decision converted what would have been "v0.2.0 is live, oops" into a failed run and a patch number.

The traceback worth reading slowly

The failure wasn't in verify logic. It was in import:

File ".../bin/agentwatch", line 3, in <module>
    from agentwatch.cli import main
  File ".../agentwatch/cli/main.py", line 71, in <module>
    from agentwatch.demo import purge_demo, render_demo, run_demo
  File ".../agentwatch/demo.py", line 22, in <module>
    from agentwatch.adapters import claude_code
  File ".../agentwatch/adapters/__init__.py", line 5, in <module>
    from agentwatch.adapters import (...
  File ".../agentwatch/adapters/a2a_proxy.py", line 36, in <module>
    from agentwatch import agent_card
  File ".../agentwatch/agent_card.py", line 26, in <module>
    from cryptography.exceptions import InvalidSignature
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'cryptography'

The release environment runs pip install -e packages/python-sdk — no extras. And cryptography in this project is an optional extra ([signing]): a hard dependency would be wrong, since most installs never sign anything.

But agent_card.py — the A2A agent-card signature verifier — imported InvalidSignature at module top. And agent_card is imported by the adapters package. Which is imported by demo. Which is imported by the CLI. So:

A plain pip install agentsec-agentwatch produced a CLI that died on --help. No signing involved. No A2A involved. Just an import chain doing what import chains do — eagerly dragging everything into memory at startup.

Every environment where this ran had cryptography present — dev setups install extras, CI quality jobs install extras. Only the release job installs bare. The one environment guaranteed to represent a real user — a clean, no-extras install — was the one that caught it.

What "optional" has to mean

The fix is small and I now consider it a rule:

def _verify_signature(public: Any, alg: str, signing_input: bytes, signature: bytes) -> bool:
    from cryptography.exceptions import InvalidSignature          # lazy
    from cryptography.hazmat.primitives import hashes
    from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric import ec, ed25519, padding, rsa
    ...

The imports moved inside the one function that actually uses them — the verification path, which is also the path that requires the extra to be present anyway. Everything above it — module load, CLI startup, adapter imports, the entire non-signing surface — no longer cares whether cryptography exists.

Then the proof, which is the part I'd never done before for an import: a test that blocks the module, then imports the CLI:

class Blocker:
    def find_spec(self, name, path=None, target=None):
        if name == "cryptography" or name.startswith("cryptography."):
            raise ModuleNotFoundError("cryptography blocked for test")
        return None

sys.meta_path.insert(0, Blocker())
import agentwatch.cli.main  # must succeed

A meta-path hook that makes cryptography unimportable, then imports the CLI against it. If anyone ever moves that import back to module top, this test goes red in CI instead of at the next release. The A2A card tests (26 of them) still pass with cryptography present, so the feature didn't move an inch.

tip: An extra is only optional if the package works without it — and "works" is checked where it's truest: a clean no-extras install importing the entry point.

Why my test suite couldn't catch this

This is the part I sat with afterward. The suite that guards packaging is solid — it enforces one version across surfaces, validates the SBOM, checks the wheel contents. But every test environment installs extras. A missing-optional-dependency bug is invisible to any environment that has the dependency — which is all of them, except the one a user gets.

The only two places this class of bug can surface:

  1. A clean install in the release pipeline — which is what verify-release is, and why it's a precondition and not a post-publish nicety.
  2. A fresh-venv install-from-the-registry check after publish — which is the human-run check that, one release later, caught the version-banner bug the pipeline couldn't catch (the CLI imported fine; it just printed the wrong number).

Between those two checks, this class of bug has nowhere left to live. That's the actual architecture I'm taking out of this: gates at the boundaries where the environment stops lying to you.

The ending that could have been

Play it back without the verify step: tag pushes, workflow builds, signs, publishes. v0.2.0 goes to PyPI with a CLI that cannot start. Every clean install — the majority case — gets a broken tool with a signed, SBOM'd, provenance-attested wheel. All the supply-chain rigor intact, delivering a package that dies on import.

Instead: a failed run, a 2-line fix (PR #495), a re-tag, and a release with 8 assets — wheel, sdist, SBOM, checksums, each with its Sigstore bundle — that all actually work. v0.2.1 shipped the same way, first try, because the class of bug was already dead.

The question worth asking of your release pipeline: what's the last thing that runs before publish, and would it catch a broken import? If the answer is "nothing, we trust the build" — your next release is already scheduled, you just don't know what it's about.

References

  • Release: agentwatch v0.2.1 on GitHub · on PyPI
  • The fix: PR #495 — lazy cryptography import · the release workflow ("refuses to publish an artifact that verify-release cannot confirm")
  • The no-extras import proof: a sys.meta_path hook that blocks cryptography and then imports the CLI — run at release time; the pattern is worth committing as a test
  • v0.2.0 field test report
  • Suite: agentsec-ecosystem — the full set of agent-security tools

articles.title: Top 5 Best US Stock Market APIs for Developers in 2026
articles.description: Building a stock market dashboard, portfolio tracker, investment research platform, or financial...
articles.body_html:
Building a stock market dashboard, portfolio tracker, investment research platform, or financial application requires reliable access to market data. A stock market API simplifies this process by providing structured access to stock prices, historical data, market indices, ETFs, and other financial information without requiring developers to maintain their own data collection infrastructure.

However, stock market APIs differ considerably in coverage, data freshness, historical depth, and integration capabilities. Some specialize in real-time exchange data, others focus on company fundamentals, while others provide access to multiple markets and asset classes through a unified interface.

Here are five US stock market APIs worth considering in 2026, including their key features, limitations, and ideal use cases.

1. NGN Market

NGN Market is a financial market intelligence platform providing developers with access to US stocks, ETFs, ADRs, indices, historical prices, and market analytics through a REST API.

The platform covers securities listed on major US exchanges, including Nasdaq and the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE), alongside market data from African exchanges, including the Nigerian Exchange (NGX).

One of NGN Market's distinguishing features is its unified API and billing structure. All supported markets, asset classes, features, and endpoints are accessible through a single API subscription, with endpoint availability determined by the selected access tier. Developers can work with US equities, ETFs, indices, and supported African market datasets without maintaining separate subscriptions for each market or data category.

Key Features and Advantages

  • Unified API and billing: Access all supported markets, asset classes, and endpoints through one API key, subscription, and shared usage allowance, subject to plan entitlements.
  • US market coverage: Retrieve data for supported Nasdaq- and NYSE-listed stocks, ETFs, ADRs, and major market indices.
  • African market coverage: Access supported African market datasets, including Nigerian equities, through the same API infrastructure.
  • Historical market data: Retrieve historical prices and index performance data, with available history depending on the access tier.
  • Market analytics: Access market movers, trending securities, market breadth, sector performance, and year-to-date performers.
  • Developer-friendly infrastructure: REST endpoints, JSON responses, Bearer authentication, pagination, and structured error handling.

Limitations

  • Standard US market data is delayed by at least 15 minutes. Live US market data is available by request only.
  • Request quotas and rate limits depend on the selected API tier.

Best for: Financial dashboards, portfolio trackers, investment research applications, stock discovery platforms, and developers building applications that require both US and African market coverage.

Documentation: NGN Market API

2. Massive (Formerly Polygon.io)

Massive, formerly Polygon.io, is a financial market data provider offering extensive US stock market coverage, historical prices, trade and quote data, and real-time streaming capabilities.

The platform is particularly relevant for developers building trading systems, market monitoring tools, and applications requiring detailed exchange-level information.

Key Features and Advantages

  • Real-time market data: Access real-time US stock prices and market updates with the appropriate data entitlements.
  • Historical trades and quotes: Retrieve granular transaction and quotation records for quantitative research and market analysis.
  • Aggregated market data: Access historical OHLCV bars across multiple time intervals.
  • WebSocket streaming: Subscribe to continuous market updates without repeatedly polling REST endpoints.
  • Corporate actions: Retrieve dividends, stock splits, and security reference information.
  • Developer ecosystem: REST APIs, SDKs, and bulk data delivery options.

Limitations

  • Certain asset classes, including stocks and indices, are organized into separate subscription products.
  • Real-time access depends on the selected data entitlements.
  • Commercial redistribution and some customer-facing applications require appropriate licensing.

Best for: Algorithmic trading research, real-time market dashboards, quantitative analysis, and applications requiring detailed US exchange data.

Documentation: Massive API

3. Financial Modeling Prep (FMP)

Financial Modeling Prep is a financial data API specializing in company fundamentals, financial statements, valuation metrics, and investment research datasets.

Its extensive financial data catalog makes it particularly useful for applications that analyze the underlying performance of publicly traded companies, rather than relying exclusively on stock prices.

Key Features and Advantages

  • Financial statements: Access income statements, balance sheets, and cash flow statements.
  • Financial ratios: Retrieve profitability, liquidity, leverage, and valuation metrics.
  • Company profiles: Access business descriptions, market capitalization, industry classifications, and related company information.
  • Historical market data: Retrieve stock price history and supported intraday datasets.
  • Earnings and research data: Access earnings information, financial news, and analyst-related datasets.
  • Fundamental analysis: Structured financial datasets support valuation models, company comparisons, and automated research workflows.

Limitations

  • Certain datasets and historical periods are restricted to specific access tiers.
  • Commercial display and redistribution may require additional licensing.
  • Less specialized in granular exchange-level trades and quotes than dedicated market data providers.

Best for: Fundamental stock screeners, company valuation tools, financial modeling applications, and investment research platforms.

Documentation: Financial Modeling Prep API

4. EODHD

EODHD, short for End of Day Historical Data, provides financial market data across numerous international exchanges, including US equities, ETFs, indices, and other supported instruments.

The platform is particularly known for its historical market data coverage, making it useful for developers building long-term financial analysis, research, and backtesting applications.

Key Features and Advantages

  • Global exchange coverage: Access supported securities across numerous international stock exchanges.
  • Historical price data: Retrieve extensive end-of-day price history for supported securities and markets.
  • Corporate actions: Access dividend information, stock splits, and adjusted historical prices.
  • Intraday data: Retrieve intraday market information for supported exchanges and intervals.
  • Fundamental datasets: Access company financial statements and related financial information.
  • Technical indicators: Retrieve common technical analysis indicators without implementing every calculation independently.

Limitations

  • Historical depth and dataset completeness vary across exchanges and securities.
  • Specialized datasets have separate access requirements.
  • Commercial usage and redistribution rights require review.
  • Applications requiring granular real-time US trade and quote feeds may need additional infrastructure.

Best for: Historical stock market analysis, international portfolio research, quantitative backtesting, and applications requiring extensive end-of-day market data.

Documentation: EODHD API

5. Alpha Vantage

Alpha Vantage provides financial market data through an API covering historical stock prices, technical indicators, company fundamentals, and other financial datasets.

The platform uses a function-based request structure, allowing developers to retrieve specific datasets through standard HTTP requests. Its selection of precomputed technical indicators makes it particularly useful for technical analysis applications.

Key Features and Advantages

  • Historical stock prices: Access daily, weekly, monthly, and supported intraday time series.
  • Technical indicators: Retrieve RSI, MACD, moving averages, Bollinger Bands, and other indicators.
  • Company fundamentals: Access company overviews, financial statements, and related metrics.
  • Multiple asset classes: Retrieve supported equity, foreign exchange, and cryptocurrency datasets.
  • Market information: Access earnings data, market news, and additional financial information.
  • Simple integration: Standard HTTP requests with JSON and CSV responses for supported functions.

Limitations

  • Free API access has restrictive request limits.
  • Higher-throughput usage and certain datasets require additional entitlements.
  • Real-time and delayed US market data have specific access requirements.
  • Developers must account for rate limits and dataset-specific restrictions.

Best for: Technical analysis dashboards, financial education tools, lightweight market research applications, and developers experimenting with financial data integrations.

Documentation: Alpha Vantage API

How to Choose the Right US Stock Market API

Selecting a stock market API depends on the specific requirements of your application. Before choosing a provider, consider the following factors:

Market and asset coverage: Determine whether the API supports the exchanges, stocks, ETFs, indices, and international markets your application needs. Exchange coverage and asset-class coverage are different considerations, so verify that the required instruments and datasets are actually available.

Data freshness: Historical research tools may work well with delayed or end-of-day prices, while trading infrastructure may require real-time quotes and streaming market updates.

Historical depth and granularity: Daily price history is sufficient for many dashboards and portfolio applications, but quantitative research may require intraday bars, individual trades, or bid-ask quotations.

API architecture and reliability: Evaluate authentication, pagination, response formats, rate limits, error handling, and documentation. Consistent conventions can simplify integration and ongoing maintenance.

Data access and licensing: Confirm that the required endpoints are available under your subscription and that the provider permits your intended commercial use, public display, caching, or redistribution.

Testing sample API responses before committing to a provider can also help identify missing fields, inconsistent identifiers, and other integration challenges early in development.

Final Thoughts

Each of these stock market APIs addresses different technical requirements.

NGN Market offers unified access to supported US and African market datasets, with stocks, ETFs, indices, and market analytics available through a single API and billing structure. Massive specializes in detailed US exchange data and real-time streaming. Financial Modeling Prep provides extensive company fundamentals and valuation information, while EODHD focuses on historical data across international markets. Alpha Vantage offers technical indicators and accessible financial time-series endpoints.

The right choice ultimately depends on the markets your application serves, the datasets it requires, and how frequently that information needs to be updated.

For developers, reviewing the documentation, testing relevant endpoints, and understanding data entitlements before integration are practical steps toward choosing an API that can support both current requirements and future development.

articles.title: The Most Dangerous Button in Your App Is “Try Again”
articles.description: A user clicks Pay.  The spinner runs for ten seconds.  Then your app displays:   Something went...
articles.body_html:
A user clicks Pay.

The spinner runs for ten seconds.

Then your app displays:

Something went wrong. Please try again.

So they do.

A few minutes later, they find two charges.

Your frontend saw a failed request. Your backend may have completed a successful payment.

Those two things can happen at the same time.

That gap is where a harmless retry becomes an expensive bug.

And it affects more than payments: orders, bookings, emails, inventory updates, and anything else that changes state.

A timeout does not mean nothing happened

Imagine this sequence:

  1. Your app sends a request to create an order.
  2. The server creates it.
  3. The connection drops before the response reaches the app.
  4. The app reports a network error.
  5. The user retries.
  6. The server creates another order.

Both requests worked on the server.

The client only received one successful response.

A timeout means the client stopped waiting. It does not prove the server stopped working.

After a connection failure, the outcome may be unknown.

Treating “unknown” as “failed” is the mistake.

Disabling the button helps—but it isn’t enough

Disabling the submit button while a request is running is good UX.

It prevents some accidental double clicks.

But it cannot protect you from every duplicate:

  • The user refreshes the page.
  • A mobile connection drops.
  • Two tabs submit the same action.
  • A client automatically retries a request.
  • A background job runs again after a worker crashes.

A frontend safeguard cannot enforce a backend guarantee.

If doing the same action twice would cause harm, the server needs a way to recognize the repeat.

Give the action an identity

Suppose a user is confirming a booking.

Instead of sending only the booking details, the client also sends an identifier for that particular confirmation attempt:

POST /bookings
Idempotency-Key: 7f09c2e1-...
Content-Type: application/json

The server can use that key to recognize another delivery of the same operation.

The intended behavior is:

First request:
Create the booking and record the result.

Retry with the same key and same payload:
Return the recorded result.

Same key with a different payload:
Reject the request.

This is an idempotency key.

The practical goal is simple:

Repeating the same operation should not create another effect.

The key identifies an operation, not the user forever. A genuinely new booking needs a new key.

The easy mistake: generating a new key on every retry

This looks reasonable:

async function submitBooking(payload) {
  return fetch("/bookings", {
    method: "POST",
    headers: {
      "Content-Type": "application/json",
      "Idempotency-Key": crypto.randomUUID(),
    },
    body: JSON.stringify(payload),
  });
}

But every call creates a new key.

If you call this function again after a timeout, the server sees a new operation. The duplicate protection cannot help.

Instead, create the key once for the intended action and reuse it when retrying that same action:

const operation = {
  key: crypto.randomUUID(),
  payload: bookingDetails,
};

async function sendBooking(operation) {
  return fetch("/bookings", {
    method: "POST",
    headers: {
      "Content-Type": "application/json",
      "Idempotency-Key": operation.key,
    },
    body: JSON.stringify(operation.payload),
  });
}

This is a simplified example. If retries must survive a refresh or app restart, the operation identity needs to survive too.

And if the user changes the booking details, decide explicitly whether that is a new operation. Do not quietly reuse the old key with different data.

The server must handle simultaneous requests

There is another trap.

You write:

Check whether the key exists.
If it does not exist, create the booking.
Save the key.

Now two requests arrive together:

Request A checks → no key found
Request B checks → no key found

Request A creates a booking
Request B creates a booking

The check exists. The duplicate still happens.

Checking and claiming an operation must be safe under concurrency.

For a database-backed operation, a common design includes:

  • A unique constraint on the key within the authenticated account and operation scope.
  • An atomic claim of the operation.
  • A stored fingerprint of the relevant request data.
  • A transaction connecting the local business change and recorded result.
  • Defined behavior when the operation is still in progress.

The exact implementation depends on your system, but “check, then insert” without concurrency protection is not enough.

Also, an idempotency key does not replace authentication or authorization. A replayed result must remain accessible only to the appropriate caller.

External side effects need their own protection

Creating a database row and charging a payment provider are different kinds of work.

Your database transaction cannot roll back a charge that already happened elsewhere.

Consider this failure:

  1. Your server sends the payment request.
  2. The provider processes it.
  3. Your server crashes before recording the result.
  4. Your worker retries.

For providers that support idempotency, reuse the corresponding stable operation key according to their documented rules.

For other effects, you may need a durable job record, deduplication, or reconciliation.

Be precise about the guarantee:

Preventing duplicate database rows does not automatically prevent duplicate emails or charges.

Every side effect deserves its own retry story.

Your error message should reflect what you know

When an outcome is uncertain, this message can push users toward a duplicate:

Payment failed. Try again.

A more accurate message might be:

We couldn’t confirm the payment status. We’re checking it now.

Your app can then query the operation’s status before inviting another submission.

You still need backend protection. Better wording alone will not solve the bug.

But the interface should help users understand what is happening instead of encouraging repeated clicks.

Test the failure after success

Most happy-path tests check:

Send request → receive success.

The interesting test checks:

Complete the action → lose the response → retry.

For a booking endpoint, test these cases:

  1. Same key, same payload: one booking exists.
  2. Two simultaneous requests with the same key: one booking exists.
  3. Same key, different payload: the request is rejected.
  4. Completed operation, lost response, then retry: the existing result is returned.
  5. Operation still running: the retry follows your documented in-progress behavior.

Also define what happens when stored keys expire. Deduplication usually has a retention window; it is not necessarily a forever guarantee.

These tests check the behavior that ordinary “endpoint returns 201” tests miss.

A useful prompt for your AI assistant

Before asking AI to add automatic retries, try this:

Review this state-changing operation for duplicate effects.

Do not modify code yet.

Identify:
1. What happens if the server completes the action
   but the client never receives the response.
2. Whether concurrent requests can duplicate the effect.
3. How the same operation is identified across retries.
4. Whether that identity survives a refresh or restart.
5. Which external side effects need separate protection.
6. What happens when an operation is in progress
   or its deduplication record expires.

Then propose the smallest safe change
and tests that simulate success followed by response loss.

State any assumptions or missing evidence.

This gives the assistant a concrete failure model to inspect.

“Add retry logic” leaves too much unsaid.

Before you ship “Try Again”

Ask one question:

If the first attempt actually succeeded, what will the second attempt do?

If the answer is “charge again,” “book again,” or “decrease stock again,” the button needs more than a loading spinner.

Retries are useful. Make the operation safe to repeat before making it easy to repeat.

Have you encountered a duplicate-action bug? What got repeated—and where did you add the protection?

articles.title: Python 3.15 just dropped. Here's everything that changed from 3.14
articles.description: Python 3.15 landed on 9 October 2026 and okay, this one is actually a lot. We got a lazy keyword for...
articles.body_html:
Python 3.15 landed on 9 October 2026 and okay, this one is actually a lot. We got a lazy keyword for imports, two new builtin types, UTF-8 as the default encoding, a real sampling profiler in the standard library, * and ** inside comprehensions, a JIT that's finally getting somewhere, and the usual pile of removals that will ruin somebody's Friday.

I went through the release notes and the deprecations page so you don't have to.

Everything below is grouped by what it means for your code, not by whatever order the changelog happened to list it. Every item has a short explanation, an example where one helps, and a Timeline line telling you when it landed, or when something you rely on stops working.

The interactive diagrams under each section are there so you can poke at the idea instead of just reading about it. Click stuff. It's the fastest way to get it.

The headline features

1. Lazy imports (PEP 810)

Slow startup is one of those problems everybody has and nobody fixes, because the usual fix is ugly: shove import statements inside functions and hope your linter doesn't yell. Python 3.15 gives you a proper answer. A new lazy soft keyword tells Python "don't actually load this module until somebody uses it."

You still write your imports at the top of the file like a normal person. Python just doesn't pay for them until the name is touched. If a run never reaches the code that needs json, json never loads.

lazy import json
lazy from pathlib import Path

print("Starting up...")              # neither module is fully imported yet

data = json.loads('{"key": "value"}')  # json loads here
p = Path(".")                          # pathlib loads here

This is huge for CLI tools, where you pay the whole import bill just to print --help, and for anything that starts a lot, like serverless functions and test runners. The load costs in the diagram above are illustrative, so don't quote them anywhere. The idea is real though: pay only for what a run touches.

How you control it:

  • Global switch: -X lazy_imports=all|normal or the PYTHON_LAZY_IMPORTS environment variable. normal is the default and only honours the lazy keyword.
  • Runtime control: sys.set_lazy_imports(), sys.get_lazy_imports(), and sys.set_lazy_imports_filter() if you want to decide per module.
  • Backport-friendly form: set __lazy_modules__ = ["json", "pathlib"] and plain import statements for those modules become lazy. This is the one to use if you still support older Pythons.

Things that will bite you:

  • Errors show up at first use, not at import time. A typo'd or missing module won't blow up on line 1 anymore, it'll blow up later. The traceback does include the original import line, so you can still find it.
  • lazy only works at module scope. Inside a function, a class, or a try/except/finally it's a SyntaxError. Star imports and __future__ imports can't be lazy either.

Timeline: available now in 3.15. Use __lazy_modules__ if you must still support older versions.

2. frozendict builtin (PEP 814)

For years the "immutable dict" move was either types.MappingProxyType (a read-only view, not actually frozen) or rolling your own. Now there's a real builtin. A frozendict can't be changed after you make it, and it's hashable as long as everything inside it is hashable, which means you can finally use one as a dict key or drop it in a set.

Two things that surprise people. It is not a dict subclass, it inherits from object. And it remembers insertion order, but equality ignores order, so two frozendicts with the same items are equal no matter how you built them.

>>> a = frozendict(x=1, y=2)
>>> a['z'] = 3
TypeError: 'frozendict' object does not support item assignment
>>> b = frozendict(y=2, x=1)
>>> hash(a) == hash(b), a == b
(True, True)

It plays nice with the rest of the stdlib: copy, decimal, json, marshal, plistlib (serialize only), pickle, pprint, and xml.etree.ElementTree all accept it, and eval()/exec() take one for globals. It also pairs well with the new json.loads(..., object_pairs_hook=frozendict, array_hook=tuple), which gives you a fully immutable parsed document. Config files that nobody can accidentally mutate. Love that.

The one migration trap: if you check isinstance(x, dict), a frozendict will fail it. Switch to isinstance(x, (dict, frozendict)), or better, check against collections.abc.Mapping.

Timeline: available now in 3.15.

3. sentinel builtin (PEP 661)

You've written this a hundred times: _MISSING = object(), then if arg is _MISSING. It works, but the repr is a useless memory address, copying it can break the identity check, and type checkers have no idea what to do with it.

sentinel is the grown-up version. You get a unique marker with a readable name. It keeps its identity when copied, works in type expressions with |, and pickles when it's importable by module and name.

MISSING = sentinel("MISSING")

def fetch(key, default=MISSING):
    ...

Flip the toggle in the diagram. The old object() trick fails all three probes, which is a pretty good argument for switching. It's most useful anywhere None is a legitimate value and you need to tell "they passed None" apart from "they passed nothing."

Timeline: available now in 3.15.

4. UTF-8 is the default encoding (PEP 686)

This is the one most likely to break something, so read it twice. open("file.txt") with no encoding= now uses UTF-8 no matter what your system locale says. Before, Python quietly used whatever your OS preferred, which on a lot of Windows machines meant cp1252. Same code, different behaviour depending on whose laptop it ran on. That's the bug class this kills.

If your files are already UTF-8, nothing changes except it now works everywhere. If you've got legacy cp1252 files and relied on the default, a bare open() will now raise a UnicodeDecodeError, or worse, decode wrong without complaining. Mess with the three selectors in the diagram to see all four outcomes.

What to do about it:

  • Always pass encoding= explicitly in code that has to run across versions.
  • encoding="locale" opts you into the system encoding on purpose (supported since 3.10).
  • Find the call sites that depend on the old default with the opt-in encoding warning, -X warn_default_encoding.
  • Need the old behaviour back for now? PYTHONUTF8=0 or -X utf8=0 restores it.

Timeline: effective in 3.15.

5. Unpacking in comprehensions (PEP 798)

Flattening a list of lists used to mean a nested comprehension that reads backwards, or itertools.chain.from_iterable, or a loop. Now * and ** work directly inside list, set, and dict comprehensions and generator expressions.

>>> lists = [[1, 2], [3, 4], [5]]
>>> [*L for L in lists]
[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

>>> dicts = [{'a': 1}, {'b': 2}, {'a': 3}]
>>> {**d for d in dicts}
{'a': 3, 'b': 2}

>>> list(x for x in (*L for L in lists))
[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

For the dict version, later keys win, which is why 'a' ends up as 3. Async generator expressions get the same treatment, so (*a async for a in agen()) is valid. It's a small quality of life change, but it's the kind you'll use weekly.

Timeline: available now in 3.15.

6. Tachyon: a sampling profiler in the stdlib (PEP 799)

Profiling in Python used to mean restart the app under cProfile, eat the slowdown, and hope you reproduce the problem. Tachyon flips that. It's a statistical sampling profiler that attaches to a process that's already running, by PID, with no restart and no code changes. Sampling rates go up to 1,000,000 Hz.

To make room for it there's a new profiling package that groups the built-in profilers:

  • profiling.tracing is the deterministic profiler, moved over from cProfile (which stays as an alias).
  • profiling.sampling is Tachyon.

Modes are attach, run, run -m, and dump, which is a one-shot stack snapshot of every thread, or of all asyncio tasks with --async-aware. You can measure wall time (the default, --mode wall), CPU time, GIL-holding time, or exception-handling time. Output formats cover pretty much every tool people actually use: --pstats, --collapsed for flame-graph tools, --flamegraph (a self-contained HTML file), --gecko for the Firefox Profiler, and --heatmap for line-level data. There's also a live top-style TUI with --live and opcode-level detail with --opcodes.

Drag the sample rate in the diagram. At 1 Hz you miss the short function completely, and that's the whole tradeoff of sampling in one picture.

Timeline: Tachyon and profiling ship in 3.15. The old pure-Python profile module is deprecated and removed in 3.17. Use profiling.tracing, which has a compatible API.

7. Frame pointers on by default (PEP 831)

This one is invisible until you need it, and then it's the whole game. CPython is now built with frame pointers on platforms that support them. In plain terms, system profilers, debuggers, crash tools, and eBPF observability can walk the native stack faster and more reliably, without guessing.

The catch is that stack unwinding is only as good as its weakest link. If you build C, C++, or Rust extensions with your own toolchain, keep frame pointers on. One native component without them can break unwinding for the whole process, which is exactly what the diagram shows when you click a layer off. The flags are exposed through sysconfig, so extension builds can inherit them. If you really want out of the CPython default, there's --without-frame-pointers.

Timeline: default from 3.15.

8. .start files for startup code (PEP 829)

Quick background. .pth files in site-packages can run arbitrary code at interpreter startup, through any line that begins with import. It's powerful and honestly kind of scary, because it's hard to audit what's running before your program even starts.

3.15 adds .start files. They hold entry points in pkg.mod:callable form, and Python calls each callable at startup. When a matching .start file exists, the import lines in the .pth file are ignored. Plain path-extension lines in .pth files don't change.

Slide the version control in the diagram to watch the .pth import line go from "works" to "ignored" to "warns."

Timeline: .start files arrive in 3.15, and import lines in .pth files are silently deprecated now. Per the 3.15 deprecations page, they're silently ignored in 3.18, and in 3.20 they produce warnings and .pth files must be utf-8-sig encoded. If you ship a package that relies on a .pth import line, you've got time, but not infinite time.

9. Stable ABI for free-threaded builds (PEP 803, 793, 820)

If you write C extensions, this matters. Until now, the stable ABI (abi3) didn't cover free-threaded CPython, so you ended up building separate wheels. 3.15 adds abi3t, a Stable ABI compatible with free-threaded builds.

The price of admission is moving to the PEP 697 type APIs and the new PyModExport_* module hook with the PySlot structure. meson-python, scikit-build-core, and Maturin already support it. You can pick it manually with the Py_TARGET_ABI3T macro. If your extension can't make the jump yet, keep building abi3 plus a separate cp315t wheel and move over later.

Timeline: available now in 3.15.

10. Safer C API at interpreter shutdown (PEP 788)

Shutting down an interpreter while another thread is still poking at it is a classic way to get deadlocks and crashes. 3.15 adds interpreter guards, interpreter views, and attach/detach APIs so extensions can say "I'm still using this, don't finalize yet."

As part of that, the PyGILState_* family is now soft deprecated. Soft deprecated means "we'd prefer you don't use this in new code," and there's no plan to remove it, so nothing breaks.

There's also a handful of other C API additions worth knowing about: PyBytesWriter (PEP 782), PyTuple_FromArray, PyArg_ParseArray, PyAnyDict_* and PyFrozenDict_*, PyObject_Dump, and the PySys_GetAttr family. Click the chips in the diagram for a one-line description of each.

Timeline: available now in 3.15; no removal scheduled.

Performance

JIT upgrade

The experimental JIT got a real glow-up this release. It now needs LLVM 21 to build, has a new tracing frontend that records the paths your code really takes, basic register allocation, more constant propagation, and reference-count elimination where it's safe. GDB and backtrace() can also unwind through JIT frames now, which makes debugging a lot less painful.

The numbers from the release notes: an 8 to 9% geometric-mean gain on pyperformance (x86-64 Linux) over the standard interpreter, and 12 to 13% on AArch64 macOS over the tail-calling interpreter. Against no-JIT builds the spread is wide, anywhere from roughly a 15% slowdown to over 100% speedup. The source text flags these figures as not final, so treat them as a vibe check and benchmark your own workload before you tell anyone it's faster.

Timeline: still experimental in 3.15.

Windows and macOS binaries

Official 64-bit Windows binaries now use the tail-calling interpreter (built with MSVC 18 / Visual Studio 2026). That's reported at a 15 to 20% geometric-mean speedup over the old switch-based interpreter, with 14% to 40% showing up across real workloads. And official macOS binaries now install free-threading support by default. So if you're on either, you got faster for free.

Standard library speedups

A bunch of boring-but-great stuff:

  • base64: encoding is about 2x faster, decoding about 3x faster.
  • Ascii85, Base85, Z85 and Base32 were rewritten in C. That's roughly two orders of magnitude faster, and the Base85 family also uses far less memory.
  • csv.Sniffer.sniff(): up to 1.6x faster delimiter detection.
  • mimalloc is the default raw allocator on free-threaded builds.
  • subprocess.Popen.wait(timeout=...) is now event-driven (pidfd_open on Linux 5.3+, kqueue on macOS/BSD) instead of a busy loop. Less CPU burned waiting around.
  • Class creation is faster thanks to shared __dict__/__weakref__ descriptors.

The GC revert

Remember the incremental garbage collector from early 3.14? It's gone. After reports of memory pressure, the team reverted to the generational GC. 3.14.5+ and 3.15 both use the generational collector.

Typing

If you live in type hints, this section is for you. Four things landed:

  • TypeForm (PEP 747): lets you annotate values that are themselves type expressions, like def cast[T](typ: TypeForm[T], value: Any) -> T: .... At runtime, TypeForm(x) just returns x.
  • Closed and extra-item TypedDict (PEP 728): closed=True forbids keys you didn't declare, and extra_items=<type> allows extras of one specific type. Play with the selector in the diagram to see what a checker would say.
  • @typing.disjoint_base (PEP 800): lets type checkers model builtins and extension types that can't be multiply inherited.
  • TypeVarTuple now accepts bound, covariant, contravariant, and infer_variance.

There's also a protocol fix. class X(P1[S], Protocol[T, T2]) with S missing now raises TypeError, and type-parameter order is inferred correctly.

Timeline: all available in 3.15.

Language and runtime changes

The small stuff that makes daily Python nicer:

  • Better error messages. Nested attribute hints (Did you mean '.inner.area' instead of '.area'?). Cross-language hints for people whose muscle memory is from JavaScript: [].push suggests .append, 'x'.toUpperCase suggests .upper, and {}.put tells you to use d[k] = v. There are also mutable-on-immutable hints for tuples and suggestions for delattr(). Pick one in the diagram.
  • More colour across the CLI: python --help, unraisable exceptions, argparse, ast, calendar, difflib, http.server, pickletools, sqlite3, timeit, tokenize, and plenty of stdlib CLI help screens.
  • bytearray.take_bytes(n=None) moves bytes out of a buffer without copying them.
  • slice is subscriptable now (it's a generic type). __slots__ can include __dict__ and __weakref__ on any class, and tuple subclasses can have any slots.
  • match statements: literal patterns accept unary plus.
  • Import deadlock fixed: per-module locks are now taken in parent-before-child order.
  • -W and PYTHONWARNINGS accept regular expressions when a field is wrapped in /.../.
  • Timestamps and timeouts accept any real number, so Decimal and Fraction work.
  • Interactive shell: completions are coloured by kind, and from x import <Tab> suggests module attributes. pdb uses the new shell too.

New and updated modules

New: math.integer (PEP 791)

Integer-specific maths functions now live in their own module instead of being mixed in with the float stuff.

Notable library updates

Module Change
asyncio TaskGroup.cancel() ends a group early without the old exception-raising boilerplate
re re.prefixmatch() / Pattern.prefixmatch() added as the explicit name for match(); match() is soft deprecated with no removal planned
tomllib TOML 1.1.0: multiline inline tables, trailing commas, \xHH and \e escapes, optional seconds
unicodedata Unicode 17.0.0; iter_graphemes(), block(), XID helpers
threading serialize_iterator, synchronized_iterator(), concurrent_tee() for sharing iterators across threads
contextlib @contextmanager used on generator/async functions now stays open across iteration or await
base64 / binascii New padded, wrapcol, ignorechars, canonical, alphabet options; Base32/Ascii85/Base85/Z85 in binascii
json array_hook parameter on load/loads
pprint expand=True for JSON-style layout; t-string support
os / pathlib os.statx() (Linux); parent_mode on os.makedirs() and Path.mkdir()
os.path realpath(strict=os.path.ALLOW_MISSING)
ssl set_groups(), post-quantum group support, set_ciphersuites(), signature-algorithm APIs
argparse suggest_on_error now defaults to True; backtick markup in help text
http.server --header/-H, --content-type, extra_response_headers
sqlite3 CLI SQL keyword, table, column, and schema tab completion
zlib adler32_combine(), crc32_combine()
unittest assertWarns/assertWarnsRegex no longer swallow non-matching warnings
tarfile Multiple extraction-filter hardening fixes (several CVEs)
array / memoryview / ctypes Complex (Zf, Zd) and half-float (e) formats
locale getdefaultlocale() un-deprecated

A few worth a closer look. re.prefixmatch() is just the honest name for what match() always did: anchor at the start of the string. People mix up match and search constantly, so the new name saves a few confused Stack Overflow questions. match() isn't going anywhere, it's only soft deprecated. Type any pattern and string into the diagram to see how prefixmatch and search differ. asyncio.TaskGroup.cancel() is the one I'd grab first if you write async code, since ending a group early used to need awkward boilerplate. And tarfile got several security fixes, so update if you handle untrusted archives.

Removed in 3.15

These were deprecated earlier and are now gone. If your CI goes red after upgrading, start here:

  • ast: constructing nodes with missing or unknown fields raises TypeError (it's been warning since 3.13).
  • collections.abc.ByteString and typing.ByteString dropped from __all__ (full removal is still due in 3.17).
  • ctypes.SetPointerType().
  • datetime.strptime() with %d and no year now raises ValueError.
  • glob.glob0() and glob.glob1().
  • http.server.CGIHTTPRequestHandler and the --cgi flag.
  • importlib.resources.files(package=...) parameter.
  • pathlib.PurePath.is_reserved(). Use os.path.isreserved() instead.
  • platform.java_ver().
  • sre_compile, sre_constants, sre_parse.
  • sysconfig.is_python_build(check_home=...).
  • C RLock arbitrary args.
  • types.CodeType.co_lnotab.
  • typing: keyword-argument NamedTuple syntax, zero-field TypedDict("TD"), and no_type_check_decorator.
  • wave: getmark(), setmark(), getmarkers().
  • zipimport.zipimporter.load_module().
  • module.__cached__ is no longer set or consulted. Use __spec__.cached.
  • C API: the PyUnicode_AsDecodedObject family, PyImport_ImportModuleNoBlock, PyWeakref_GetObject, PySys_ResetWarnOptions, and the Py_GetPath / Py_GetPrefix / Py_GetExecPrefix / Py_GetProgramFullPath / Py_GetProgramName / Py_GetPythonHome initialization getters. Use PyConfig_Get for those.

The removal calendar

This is the part to screenshot. What's deprecated, and when it goes. Plan migrations against this table, and use the search box in the diagram to check if your own imports show up.

Removal What goes
3.16 asyncio policy system (AbstractEventLoopPolicy, DefaultEventLoopPolicy, Windows*EventLoopPolicy, get/set_event_loop_policy) and asyncio.iscoroutinefunction(); bitwise ~True / ~False; array type code 'u'; logging handlers using strm; mimetypes.add_type() with undotted extensions (becomes ValueError); __loader__ taken into account by the import system; functools.reduce keyword args in the Python implementation; shutil.ExecError; symtable.Class.get_methods; sys._enablelegacywindowsfsencoding(); sysconfig.expand_makefile_vars(); TarFile.tarfile; bundled libmpdec (C)
3.17 profile module; collections.abc.ByteString and typing.ByteString; datetime.strptime() with %e and no year; webbrowser.MacOSXOSAScript; tkinter.Variable.trace_variable()/trace()/trace_vdelete()/trace_vinfo(); non-ASCII names in encodings.normalize_encoding(); typing._UnionGenericAlias; -b / -bb become no-ops; PyConfig.bytes_warning (C)
3.18 Boolean values accepted as file descriptors; Decimal 'N' format specifier; import lines in .pth files ignored (PEP 829); private C helpers (_PyBytes_Join, _PyUnicodeWriter_*, _PyLong_New, and others)
3.19 ctypes implicit MSVC struct layout from _pack_ without _layout_; hashlib string= keyword; http.cookies js_output(); imaplib.IMAP4.file assignment; PEP 456 external hash definition (C)
3.20 __version__ / version / VERSION attributes in about two dozen stdlib modules (use sys.version_info); abstract ast node instantiation; isinstance()/issubclass() on non-runtime_checkable protocols inheriting from runtime-checkable ones; struct.Struct.__new__ without format; C: _PyObject_CallMethodId, _PyObject_GetAttrId, _PyUnicode_FromId, PyComplexObject.cval, Py_MATH_El, Py_MATH_PIl
No date datetime.utcnow() / utcfromtimestamp(), logging.warn(), threading camelCase aliases, codecs.open(), os.path.commonprefix(), urllib.parse.split*() helpers, typing.Text, argparse.FileType, ssl.PROTOCOL_* constants, shutil.rmtree(onerror=), and more

The 3.16 column is the one that'll hurt most people. The asyncio policy system is going, and a lot of older async code touches it without the author even knowing. Check that one first.

New deprecations introduced in 3.15

base64.b64decode() / urlsafe_b64decode() accepting + and / with an alternative alphabet; the -b/-bb CLI flags; runtime warnings on importing ByteString; hashlib string=; http.cookies.*.js_output(); imaplib.IMAP4.file; the __version__ attributes; webbrowser.MacOSXOSAScript; abstract ast node instantiation; Struct.__new__/__init__ misuse.

Soft deprecations (no removal planned)

re.match() / Pattern.match() (prefer prefixmatch() in new code, keep match() if you support older versions); struct codes 'F'/'D' (prefer 'Zf'/'Zd'); PyGILState_*; the PyType_FromSpec* family (prefer PySlot / PyType_FromSlots); and several legacy C macros.

Porting checklist: what could break your code

Tick these off in the diagram as you go. It remembers your progress in your browser, when the page lets it.

  1. Default encoding is UTF-8. Audit every open(), read_text(), and write_text() without encoding=. This is the big one.
  2. argparse: suggest_on_error is now True. Also, with add_argument('-f', '-foo'), dest is now 'foo' (it used to be 'f'). Pass dest= explicitly to keep the old name.
  3. base64.urlsafe_b64decode() no longer requires padding. Pass padded=True for the old strictness.
  4. unittest: assertWarns no longer hides non-matching warnings, so tests may now leak warnings that were previously masked. Your suite might get noisier without anything being newly broken.
  5. sqlite3.connect(): every parameter except database is keyword-only, and the first parameters of create_function, create_aggregate, and the handler setters are positional-only.
  6. resource.RLIM_INFINITY is always positive now. Passing the old negative values is deprecated.
  7. importlib.metadata raises MetadataNotFound instead of returning empty metadata.
  8. array.typecodes is now a tuple, not a str.
  9. ctypes complex types changed their _type_ codes to Zf, Zd, Zg.
  10. venv on POSIX creates a real lib64 directory instead of a lib64 -> lib symlink.
  11. hashlib constructors like hashlib.md5 always exist as attributes, even without backend support.
  12. Build systems: keep the frame-pointer flags from sysconfig, and note that libmpdec no longer falls back to the bundled copy implicitly.

Build and platform notes

For people who package or compile Python:

  • New --with-missing-stdlib-config=FILE lets distributors ship custom "this module is packaged separately" messages.
  • New --with-pymalloc-hugepages plus PYTHON_PYMALLOC_HUGEPAGES=1 at runtime enables 2 MiB huge-page arenas.
  • mmap.set_name() annotates anonymous mappings on Linux 5.17+.

So what does it actually mean?

3.15 isn't one giant headline. It's three shifts landing together.

Startup and observability finally got real attention. lazy imports, Tachyon, frame pointers, and JIT unwinding all point the same way: Python is getting easier to speed up and easier to diagnose in production, without rewriting anything.

Python grew the primitives people were hand-rolling for years. frozendict and sentinel are the "why didn't we have this already" additions. Expect to delete some homemade helper classes.

Encoding and import behaviour got stricter and more predictable. UTF-8 by default, .start files, and a long, dated list of removals. Less "works on my machine," more "works the same everywhere."

If you only do one thing this week, run your test suite on 3.15 with -X warn_default_encoding and -W error::DeprecationWarning. Then check your code against the 3.16 column of the removal calendar. Future you will be thankful.

Sources: What's new in Python 3.15 · Python 3.15 deprecations · PEP 790: 3.15 release schedule

articles.title: Time Zone Conversion: 7 Mistakes That Break Schedules and Timestamps
articles.description: Time zones are a classic source of bugs: meetings scheduled an hour off, reports that miss a day,...
articles.body_html:
Time zones are a classic source of bugs: meetings scheduled an hour off, reports that miss a day, jobs that run twice. Most of the pain comes from a small set of avoidable mistakes.

1. Storing local times without a zone

A value like 2026-03-08 02:30 is ambiguous. Store instants in UTC (or as an ISO 8601 string with an offset, such as 2026-03-08T02:30:00Z) and convert to local time only when displaying it.

2. Using abbreviations

CST can mean Central Standard Time, China Standard Time, or Cuba Standard Time. IST can be India, Ireland, or Israel. Use IANA names such as America/Chicago, Asia/Kolkata, or Europe/London, which are unambiguous and carry the daylight saving rules.

3. Confusing offsets with zones

An offset like UTC-5 is a fixed number. A zone like America/New_York is a set of rules that changes between UTC-5 and UTC-4 during the year. Recurring events need a zone, not just an offset.

4. Ignoring daylight saving transitions

  • When clocks spring forward, a local hour doesn't exist (2:30 AM may be skipped).
  • When clocks fall back, a local hour happens twice, so a local time can map to two different instants.
  • Not all places observe DST, and the rules change by government decision.

5. Assuming whole-hour offsets

India is UTC+5:30, Nepal is UTC+5:45, and some regions use half-hour offsets. Code that assumes whole hours will be wrong for millions of people.

6. Adding 24 hours to mean 'tomorrow'

On a DST change a local day can be 23 or 25 hours long. Use a date library to add calendar days in a specific zone.

7. Scheduling recurring meetings in UTC

A meeting at 09:00 in New York stays at 09:00 local all year, which is a different UTC time in summer and winter. Store the zone and local time for recurring events.

Rules of thumb

Store UTC, store IANA zone names when the local time matters, convert at the edges, and use a maintained library instead of hand-written offset math.

Frequently asked questions

What is the best way to store dates and times?

Store instants in UTC (or ISO 8601 with an offset) and convert to the user's time zone only when displaying.

Why shouldn't I use EST or IST?

Abbreviations are ambiguous and don't encode daylight saving rules. Use IANA zone names like America/New_York.

How do I convert between time zones?

Convert the local time to a UTC instant using the source zone's rules, then express that instant in the target zone.

Which time zones use half-hour offsets?

Examples include India (UTC+5:30), and Nepal uses UTC+5:45.
